The live panel shows the tide now and the next high and low tide for three Koh Samui points: Chaweng on the east coast, Nathon on the west and Thong Krut in the south-west. Samui's tide is mainly diurnal: on most days there is one high and one low, about 50 minutes later each day, with a range of about 0.4 m on small-tide days and up to about 1.5–2 m on the biggest. The north and west beaches (Bophut, Bang Rak, Maenam, Lipa Noi, Bang Por, Bang Kao) turn into shallow flats at low tide, so swim there around high tide.

Switch between the three points to see the local times. Tide times around Samui differ by less than an hour between coasts, and heights by a few centimetres; what changes is the shape of the seabed, which decides how far the water retreats. Daytime low tides (between about 06:30 and 18:00) are the ones that empty the shallow beaches. Heights are astronomical predictions from a global tide model, not live gauge readings, so strong wind, low pressure and heavy rain can push the real water level higher or lower by 10–30 cm.

Good to know: these tide times are for beach planning only. They are not for navigation; skippers should use official nautical charts and tide tables.

How the tide works on Samui

Most of the world's coasts have two high tides and two low tides a day. The Gulf of Thailand is different: its shape and size amplify the once-a-day (diurnal) part of the tide, so Samui usually gets a single high and a single low in each 24 hours or so. Because the moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, the tide does too, and the whole pattern slides through the clock over a few weeks.

The size of the tide changes in a cycle of about two weeks. In a diurnal tide like Samui's, the biggest ranges come when the moon is furthest north or south of the equator, and the smallest when it crosses the equator. On the smallest days the water barely moves and the timing can wander by several hours; on the biggest days the sea runs well out at low tide and right up the beach at high tide. The full and new moon matter less here than on coasts with twice-daily tides.

Why the water goes so far out

The north and west coasts of Samui are fringed by wide, almost flat sand and mud flats, some of them with patches of rock and dead coral. A drop of a metre in the water level on a slope that falls only a few centimetres every metre exposes tens of metres of seabed. At Bang Por, a stony flat of 50 m or more appears at low tide; at Lipa Noi and Maenam the water can be knee-deep a long way out. The east coast beaches (Chaweng, Lamai) shelve more steeply, so the same tide moves the waterline far less.

Why tide apps disagree

Two tide apps can show the same tide times with very different heights, for example a range of 0.2 m to 1.7 m in one and -0.5 m to +0.7 m in another. Both can be right. One measures from a low reference level (chart datum), so its heights are always positive; the other measures from mean sea level, so low tides show as negative numbers. What matters for the beach is the difference between high and low on the same day and the times, which agree closely. Heights also come from global tide models rather than a local gauge, so treat them as accurate to a few tens of centimetres.

The pattern is shared with neighbouring Koh Phangan, a few kilometres north. In short: from March to September low tides fall in daylight, so plan north- and west-coast swims for the afternoon or evening; from October to February the beaches are full by day.

Shallow at low tide

Bophut, Bang Rak, Maenam, Bang Por, Laem Yai, Lipa Noi, Taling Ngam and Bang Kao all go shallow at low tide. On these beaches, check the panel above and plan your swim for the two or three hours around high tide. At Lipa Noi and Taling Ngam the shallow, warm water at mid tide is ideal for small children; at Bang Por and Bang Kao the low-tide flats are stony, so wear shoes.

Swimmable at most tides

Chaweng, the centre of Lamai, Silver Beach and the middle of Choeng Mon have enough slope to swim at most states of the tide. In return they face the north-east monsoon, so from October to January the problem is waves and red flags, not shallow water. See the Koh Samui beaches guide for every beach.

Low-tide specials

At low tide a sandbar runs from Choeng Mon to Koh Fan Noi, the islet at the north end of the bay, and you can walk across. Go on a falling tide and come back well before the water turns, because the sandbar floods from both sides. On the exposed flats, look at what the tide leaves behind but don't collect shells or animals.

Planning a beach day around the tide

  • Swimming on the north and west coasts: aim for the two or three hours either side of high tide. From March to September that usually means late afternoon or evening; from October to February, the middle of the day.
  • Toddlers: the shallow, warm water at mid tide on Lipa Noi or Maenam is ideal. At low tide the sea may be a long walk away.
  • Snorkelling from the shore: Laem Yai and Coral Cove are better from mid to high tide, when there is water over the rocks. See the snorkelling guide.
  • Beach walks and photos: low tide exposes the sand patterns and rock pools on the north coast, and the Choeng Mon sandbar.
  • Sunset on the west coast: at Lipa Noi and Taling Ngam a high tide at sunset puts the water right at your feet; at low tide the flats reflect the sky. Both look good. See sunset spots.
  • East-coast surf: in the monsoon, a high tide plus big waves can push water to the back of the beach at Chaweng and Lamai. Keep bags and children well up the sand.

Tides for boats, kayaks and piers

Tides change how boat trips run, though rarely whether they run.

  • Pig Island and Koh Tan: boats land on the beach at Koh Madsum and anchor near the reef at Koh Tan. At very low tide the boat stops further out, the wade ashore is longer, and the captain may swap the order of the stops so the reef is snorkelled at a better depth. Our Pig Island speedboat tour runs at any tide. Our sister site pigislandkohsamui.com covers the southern islands in more detail.
  • Ang Thong: the landing beaches at Koh Mae Ko and Koh Wua Talab are steeper, so the tide matters less. The guide picks the snorkelling reef partly by tide; see the Ang Thong speedboat tour.
  • Thong Krut and the west-coast piers: at very low tide, boarding a longtail can mean a short wade; wear sandals you don't mind getting wet.
  • Kayak and SUP: launch on the north and west coasts from mid to high tide, or you will be dragging the board across the flats. Watch for offshore wind, which can carry you out faster than you can paddle back. See kayak and SUP on Koh Samui.
  • Private charters: skippers anchor with up to 2 m of tide in mind and plan bay visits around it. Ask when you book a private speedboat.

A last tip: the tide times on this page slip by roughly 50 minutes a day, so a perfect high-tide swim at 15:00 today will be closer to 16:00 tomorrow. Check again each morning of your stay rather than relying on yesterday's times.

Full moon, spring tides and party nights

On coasts with two tides a day, the biggest (spring) tides come just after the full and new moon. Samui's mainly once-a-day tide follows the moon's position north or south of the equator instead, so the biggest tides of the month often fall a few days away from the full moon, not on it. The next Full Moon Party on Koh Phangan, on Tuesday 24 November 2026, falls in the season when low tides come at night or in the evening and high tides by day. If you are heading to Haad Rin, the tide matters less than the sea state; check sea conditions and our Full Moon Party from Samui guide.

Low-tide warnings

  • Getting cut off: sandbars, like the one to Koh Fan Noi, flood from both sides. Turn back before the tide turns.
  • Sea urchins and coral: the low-tide flats at Bang Por, Bang Kao and parts of Lamai's north end hide urchins and sharp coral. Wear reef shoes and don't walk on living coral.
  • Cuts: coral and rock cuts infect easily in the tropics. Clean them with fresh water and antiseptic and watch for redness.
  • Rocks in surf: high tide plus monsoon waves makes rocky headlands dangerous; a tourist was swept off the rocks at the Lad Koh viewpoint in November 2024.
  • Jellyfish: they drift into the shallows in calm water. Vinegar for at least 30 seconds on a sting, and call 1669.
  • Not for navigation: the times here are for planning beach days, not for steering a boat.

More safety advice is in beach and swimming safety.
